examples.before:
troupe.yml:
prompt: file:prompt.txt  # LF text include
notes: file:notes.txt  # CRLF text include
model: opus

prompt.txt:
You are a helpful coder.
Be brief.
examples.input: `config set prompt 42` (`prompt` is a text include using LF line endings)

results.1:
exit 0, no output; prompt.txt now holds only the following, with no line break at the end:
42
results.2: exit 3; prompt.txt is unchanged. Both arms refuse this, with differently worded messages: "troupe: write refused: /theatre/.troupe/prompt.txt: a text include can only be set to a string" / "troupe: prompt: text include .troupe/prompt.txt can only be set to a string"
results.3: exit 3; prompt.txt is unchanged. All three arms refuse this, with differently worded messages, e.g. "troupe: prompt: is the text of .troupe/prompt.txt; VALUE must be a string"

examples.before:
prompt.txt:
You are a helpful coder.
Be brief.
examples.input: `config set prompt '{a: 1, b: [x, y]}'` then `config get prompt`

results.2: set: exit 3 in both arms ("…can only be set to a string"); the file is unchanged. get prints the original two lines "You are a helpful coder." and "Be brief."
results.3: set: exit 3 in all three arms ("…must be a string"); the file is unchanged. get prints the original two lines "You are a helpful coder." and "Be brief."

examples.input: `config set notes '"new one\nnew two\n"'` (`notes` is a text include using CRLF line endings)

results.1:
exit 0; notes.txt now reads, with the CRLF endings kept:
new one
new two
results.2:
exit 0; notes.txt now reads, with the CRLF endings kept:
new one
new two
results.3:
exit 0; notes.txt now reads, with the CRLF endings kept:
new one
new two

results.1: exit 3; nothing changed. Message: "troupe: notes: text include /theatre/.troupe/notes.txt uses CRLF line endings, so VALUE must be a string; no file changed"
results.2: exit 3 in both arms; nothing changed. The message says a text include can only be set to a string.
results.3: exit 3 in all three arms; nothing changed. The message says the value must be a string.

context.in_practice: On route 1, whether a non-text value is accepted depends on the file's line endings, which users can't see. The same `config set prompt 42` succeeds on an LF file and fails on a CRLF file. When it succeeds, the old text is replaced with the typed characters and no warning is shown. On routes 2 and 3, every non-text value is refused and the file is left alone, whatever its line endings. Routes 2 and 3 behaved the same in every command; their arms differ only in the wording of the error message.
context.stakes: Text includes are settings whose value lives in a separate text file. This decides what happens when someone runs `config set` on one with a number, a true/false value or a structure such as `{a: 1}` instead of plain text. Either that file's text is quietly replaced with whatever was typed, or the command is refused and nothing changes.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 accepts anything on LF files but can silently replace a prompt with a stray number or structure, and its rule depends on line endings. Routes 2 and 3 apply one rule everywhere (text only) but make users quote anything that looks like a number, true/false or a structure.

plan_why: Writes an integer and then a mapping into an LF text include, then a string and a boolean into a CRLF text include. This shows whether non-strings are written as typed or refused with exit 3, and whether CRLF endings are kept.
routes: Any VALUE on an LF target (non-strings written as typed); refuse only a non-string for a CRLF target. Reworked from an early draft that refused mappings and lists
Only strings (otherwise exit 3); CRLF endings of the target are preserved
